The Italian Reformation
ih-TAL-yan ref-or-MAY-shun
proper noun
The recovery of the gospel in Italy in the sixteenth century, crushed by Rome and the Inquisition, its exiles scattered through Reformed Europe.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

The Italian Reformation was the brief and bright dawning of the gospel in sixteenth-century Italy, in the very shadow of Rome, before it was crushed by the Inquisition. Its chief lights were Peter Martyr Vermigli, the learned reformer who fled to teach at Strasbourg, Oxford, and Zurich, and Bernardino Ochino, the famed Capuchin preacher who left his order for the gospel; about them gathered a circle at Naples under Juan de Valdés, where many noble souls came to taste justification by faith alone. Behind them stood the ancient endurance of the Waldensians, the “poor men of Lyons,” who in the valleys of Piedmont had held to a simpler faith for three centuries before Luther, and who in 1532 cast in their lot with the Reformation. But Rome would not suffer the light. The Roman Inquisition, set up afresh in 1542, hunted the evangelicals through the peninsula; the Index forbade their books; the Waldensian valleys were drenched in blood in massacre after massacre. The Italian Reformation was crushed at home, yet its exiles enriched the churches of Geneva, Zurich, and England, carrying their gifts where they could freely worship. They overcame by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony, and loved not their lives unto the death (Rev 12:11); for all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution (2Ti 3:12); and of such, of whom the world was not worthy, they wandered in deserts, in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth (Heb 11:37–38).

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The gospel's brief dawn in Italy was crushed by Roman corruption and the Inquisition, yet its martyrs and exiles enriched the Reformed church.

expand to see more

The corruption the Italian Reformation suffered under was the Roman Church itself, which would not endure the recovered gospel in its own homeland. When justification by faith began to be preached at Naples and Lucca and through the peninsula, Rome answered not with Scripture but with the sword. The Roman Inquisition was newly armed in 1542 to hunt down the evangelicals; the Index of forbidden books strangled their writings; and the ancient Waldensian valleys of Piedmont, which had kept a purer faith for centuries before Luther, were given over to massacre. This persecution the dictionary names as the corruption of a church that defended its errors with blood rather than confess them and be reformed.

Yet the LORD turned the cruelty of Rome to the enriching of His church. The exiles driven out of Italy — Vermigli, Ochino, and many another — carried their learning and their faith to Geneva, Zurich, Strasbourg, and England, strengthening the Reformation where it could stand. The blood of the Waldensian martyrs, of whom the world was not worthy, became seed; for they overcame by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, and loved not their lives unto the death. The dictionary honours these martyrs and exiles, and names the persecution that scattered them for what it was: the corruption of Rome resisting the gospel of grace.
